messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.02 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.15 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.01 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Input: Piezoelectric energy harvester (Ip, f, Cp, Rleak = 20MΩ).
    *   Goal: Power a load RL (various conditions S1-S6) with a storage capacitor at "out".
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (Settle mean)
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (Absolute max)
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (Ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.15\text{ s}$ (Startup time)
        *   $dv \le 0.01\text{ V}$ (Stability)
    *   Piezo Voltage (open circuit): $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$ at S1.
    *   Problem with Reference (FBR):
        *   S2 (Heavy load): Fails $v_{avg}$ (1.76V < 1.8V).
        *   S3 (Strong excitation): Fails $v_{max}$ (5.72V > 3.6V).
        *   S4 (Weak excitation): Fails $v_{avg}$ (1.51V < 1.8V).
        *   S5/S6: Ripple and Startup issues.
        *   Ripple is generally too high (20-80mV vs 20mV limit).

    *   The open-circuit voltage is quite low ($\sim 3.2\text{ V}$ peak), which is very close to the target $1.8\text{V}$ to $3.6\text{V}$ range.
    *   A Full Bridge Rectifier (FBR) loses $2 \times V_{diode} \approx 0.5\text{V}$ (using DSCH).
    *   $V_{out} \approx V_{oc} - 0.5\text{V}$. If $V_{oc}$ drops (S4), $V_{out}$ falls below 1.8V.
    *   If $V_{oc}$ increases (S3), $V_{out}$ exceeds 3.6V.
    *   The ripple is high because the storage capacitor is either too small or the rectification is inefficient.

    *   *Synchronous Switching Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI)*: This increases the harvested energy by flipping the voltage across $C_p$ using an inductor and a switch at the peaks. This increases $v_{avg}$ and $t_{up}$.
    *   *Zener Clamp*: Necessary to keep $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ for S3.
    *   *Low-loss Rectification*: Using SYNC switches instead of diodes or using SSHI.
    *   *Storage Capacitor*: Needs to be large enough to reduce ripple.

    *   **Design 1: SSHI (Parallel/Standard) with FBR and Zener Clamp.**
        *   Inductor L1 and Switch S1 used to invert the piezo voltage at peaks.
        *   Rectifier (FBR) to charge $C_{out}$.
        *   Zener (DZ33) to clamp $V_{out}$ to 3.3V.
        *   $C_{out}$ for ripple and stability.
        *   *Wait*: The prompt says "S" switches are available. Let's try an SSHI-like topology.
        *   Actually, the simplest way to boost voltage and efficiency is SSHI.
        *   SSHI setup: L and S in parallel with the piezo, switching at extrema.
        *   Then a rectifier to the load.

    *   **Design 2: Synchronous Rectification (Active Bridge).**
        *   Replace diodes with switches controlled by SYNC.
        *   This eliminates the diode drop, helping S2 and S4.
        *   Zener clamp for S3.

    *   **Design 3: SSHI with Integrated Rectification.**
        *   Using a simpler "Half-Bridge" SSHI or a charge pump approach if applicable.
        *   Let's stick to a well-known SSHI + Rectifier.

    *   Piezo: `pzp`, `pzn`.
    *   L-C Inversion: `L1` between `pzp` and `n1`, `S1` between `n1` and `pzn`.
    *   Rectification: FBR (`D1`...`D4`) from `pzp`/`pzn` to `out`.
    *   Clamp: `D_zener` from `0` to `out`.
    *   Filter: `C_out` from `out` to `0`.
    *   SYNC `G1`: `edges="both"`, `ton` calculated for $L \cdot C_p$ inversion. $T_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$. For $L=10\text{mH}, C_p=25\text{nF}, T_{on} \approx 25\mu\text{s}$.

    *   Instead of FBR, use a synchronous rectifier. But SYNC is limited to 2 controllers.
    *   One SYNC for SSHI, one for rectification? That's tight.
    *   Alternative: Use the SSHI to boost the voltage, and use a high-efficiency rectifier.

    *   **Proposal 1: SSHI + FBR + Zener.**
        *   SSHI: `L1` (pzp-n1), `S1` (n1-pzn), `G1` (both, phase 0).
        *   FBR: `D1` (pzp-out), `D2` (pzn-out), `D3` (0-pzp), `D4` (0-pzn). (Note: "return diodes have their anode on ground").
        *   Clamp: `DZ1` (0-out).
        *   Cap: `Cout` (out-0).
        *   Rationale: SSHI increases energy extraction (helps S2, S4), Zener prevents overvoltage (S3), large Cout reduces ripple.

    *   **Proposal 2: SSHI + Half-Bridge (Simplified).**
        *   If the piezo is balanced around 0V, a half-bridge might work, but the FBR is safer.
        *   Let's try a "Synchronous Rectifier" approach. If we use `S` switches for rectification, we need a SYNC to trigger them. But the SYNC for SSHI is already at the peaks.
        *   Let's try an SSHI with a more optimized Capacitor value.

    *   **Proposal 3: Standard FBR + Zener + Very Large Capacitor (Baseline Improvement).**
        *   The FBR failed S2/S4 because of diode drops.
        *   Let's try a "Charge Pump" or "Voltage Doubler" if $V_{oc}$ is too low.
        *   Wait, $V_{oc}$ is 3.2V. $3.2 - 0.5 = 2.7\text{V}$. Why did S4 fail?
        *   S4: $I_p = 30\mu\text{A}, f = 100\text{Hz}, C_p = 25\text{nF}$. $V_{oc} = 30\mu / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{n}) \approx 1.91\text{V}$.
        *   $1.91\text{V} - 0.5\text{V} = 1.41\text{V}$. This is why S4 fails.
        *   We *must* boost the voltage for S4. SSHI is the way.

    *   L1: 10mH
    *   S1: pzp to pzn (no, that shorts the piezo).
    *   Correct SSHI: $L$ in series with $S$ across the piezo.
    *   `L1` (pzp to n1), `S1` (n1 to pzn).
    *   SYNC `G1`: `edges="both"`, `ton` around $20-30\mu\text{s}$.
    *   FBR:
        *   D1: pzp -> out
        *   D2: pzn -> out (Incorrect! For FBR: pzp -> out, pzn -> out is not possible. Correct FBR: D1[pzp, out], D2[pzn, out] is for a center-tapped or specific config. Standard: D1[pzp, out], D2[pzn, out] is wrong).
        *   Wait, the prompt says: "full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]".
        *   Let's check:
            *   D1: pzp -> out
            *   D2: pzn -> out
            *   D3: 0 -> pzp
            *   D4: 0 -> pzn
        *   This means when pzp is positive, D1 conducts. When pzn is positive, D2 conducts. When pzp is negative, D3 conducts (pzp to 0). When pzn is negative, D4 conducts (pzn to 0).
        *   Wait, the "full bridge" definition provided: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`.
        *   Let's trace:
            *   pzp > 0: current flows pzp -> out -> load -> 0 -> pzn. (D1 and D4 conduct).
            *   pzp < 0: current flows pzn -> out -> load -> 0 -> pzp. (D2 and D3 conduct).
            *   This is a correct full bridge.

    *   `S1` (pzp, pzn), `ctrl`="G1". No, that's a short.
    *   `L1` (pzp, n1), `S1` (n1, pzn), `ctrl`="G1". This is the correct series L-S combination.
    *   `G1`: `edges`="both", `ton`=3e-5, `phase`=0.

    *   S3: $V_{oc} = 100\mu / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{n}) \approx 6.36\text{V}$.
    *   SSHI will boost this further.
    *   Zener `DZ1` (0, out) will clamp it to 3.3V.

    *   $v_{pp} \le 0.02\text{V}$ is very tight.
    *   $C_{out}$ must be large. Let's try 22uF or 47uF. Max allowed is 47uF.

    *   Design 1: SSHI + FBR + Zener + Large C.
    *   Design 2: SSHI + FBR + Large C (No Zener, just to see if it's needed or if we can use a different clamp). No, Zener is safer for S3.
    *   Design 3: Synchronous Rectifier (using Switches) instead of FBR.
        *   `S2` (pzp, out), `S3` (pzn, out), `S4` (0, pzp), `S5` (0, pzn).
        *   This requires a SYNC controller to flip them.
        *   `G2`: `edges="both"`, `ton`=0.001 (long), `phase`=0.
        *   But we already used `G1` for SSHI. We can have at most 2 SYNCs.
        *   So, Design 3: SSHI (G1) + Synchronous Rectifier (G2).

    *   `L1` (pzp, n1), `S1` (n1, pzn), `ctrl`="G1".
    *   `S2` (pzp, out), `S3` (pzn, out), `S4` (0, pzp), `S5` (0, pzn), `ctrl`="G2".
    *   `G1`: SSHI (short pulses at peaks).
    *   `G2`: Rectification (long pulses).
    *   Wait, the rectifier switches `S2-S5` need to be complementary.
    *   `S2` (pzp, out) and `S4` (0, pzn) should be ON when pzp > 0.
    *   `S3` (pzn, out) and `S5` (0, pzp) should be ON when pzp < 0.
    *   This requires two different SYNC settings (phase 0 and phase 0.5). But we only have 2 SYNCs total.
    *   One SYNC for SSHI, one for... something else.
    *   If we use the SYNC for the bridge, we can't have the SSHI.
    *   Let's stick to the FBR for the rectifier in Design 1 and 2.

    *   S4: $V_{oc} \approx 1.9\text{V}$. FBR loss $\approx 0.5\text{V}$. $V_{out} \approx 1.4\text{V}$.
    *   SSHI boosts the effective $V_{oc}$ by reducing the voltage across $C_p$ during the discharge phase.
    *   With SSHI, the voltage delivered to the rectifier can be significantly higher than $V_{oc}$.
    *   $V_{out} \approx 2 \cdot V_{oc} - \text{losses}$.
    *   This should easily push S4 over 1.8V.

    *   $C_{out}$ max is 47uF. Let's start with 22uF.
    *   `L1` value: $10\text{mH}$ is a typical starting point.
    *   `ton`: $3.14 \cdot \sqrt{10\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 25\mu\text{s}$.
